prompt.context: Our client is a Canadian-based Timber Company in 2009. It primarily makes 2x4s, and the U.S. Residential construction market is, by far, the largest consumer of these products. It also sells sawdust, which is a derivative of 2x4 production. The housing crash has just happened, and demand has dropped precipitously. The client is in dire financial straits and bleeding cash. Current internal projections state that we can run the company for only 6 months longer at the current rate of cash loss.
prompt.question: What can we do to turn around the company?

clarifying_info.q: Is the company privately or publicly owned?
clarifying_info.a: Privately owned; the family has cash to spend if it makes sense.

clarifying_info.q: What does the production process look like?
clarifying_info.a: 2-step process: trees are cut down, sent to a saw mill, then sent on trucks to a transportation warehouse.
All equipment is brand new, employees are optimized, and we are running at full capacity. Trucks are new and fuel efficient. We are the leanest, most efficient operation in the business.
We hold 1/3 market share; the rest of the industry is small, fragmented, and much higher on the cost curve.

clarifying_info.q: What is our land cost structure?
clarifying_info.a: We lease land for trees from the Canadian government; the cost is negligible — we pay per tree cut down.

clarifying_info.q: How do we distribute our product?
clarifying_info.a: 2x4s are sent by truck to the closest warehouse in Chicago, and buyers purchase from there. It is a commodity market — all products are the same.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other revenue streams we could pursue?
clarifying_info.a: We cannot utilize other revenue streams because our firm is not set up for them and doing so would be prohibitively expensive.

framework: 1. Revenue — (a) Number of sales: existing customers, new customers; (b) Price: commodity good, limited pricing power
2. Costs — (a) Raw materials; (b) Manufacturing; (c) Transportation; (d) Storage; (e) Labor
3. Product Mix — (a) Existing mix; (b) Expansion opportunities (e.g., new geographies, new products)
4. Cash Injection — (a) Outside funding (family, banks, investors); (b) Selling non-core assets
5. Market Dynamics — (a) Competitor positioning; (b) Demand outlook and recovery timing

questions.prompt: Walk through revenue levers. Can we increase sales volume or price?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize this is a commodity market — pricing power is essentially zero. New customers are hard to acquire quickly. Existing customers are cutting back due to the housing crash. Encourage the candidate to explore new geographies (e.g., Mexico) or alternative buyers, but ultimately the interviewer should push back: entering a new market takes too long given the 6-month runway.

questions.prompt: Walk through cost levers. Where can we cut costs?
questions.guidance: The company is already the lowest-cost operator: brand-new equipment, optimized workforce, fuel-efficient trucks. There is essentially no fat to cut. Candidate should identify all cost buckets (raw materials, manufacturing, transportation, storage, labor) but should conclude that meaningful cost reduction is not feasible given the already-optimized operation.

questions.prompt: Are there new products or revenue streams we could add?
questions.guidance: Candidate may suggest wood pellets, paper pulp, furniture lumber, or other wood derivatives from sawdust or offcuts. Interviewer should shoot these down individually: the firm is not set up for them and conversion would be prohibitively expensive given the 6-month cash runway.

questions.prompt: Given that operational fixes are exhausted, what strategic options remain?
questions.guidance: This is the crux of the case. A strong candidate reaches the insight that no internal operational lever can stop the cash bleed and pivots to external solutions: (1) Wait it out — as the lowest-cost player with 1/3 market share, smaller high-cost competitors will fail first; the resulting supply drop will push prices back up; the client is literally best positioned to be the last firm standing. (2) Family cash injection — inject capital directly to extend the runway, or use family cash to acquire distressed competitors cheaply, consolidating market share for the recovery. (3) Government bailout — appeal to the Canadian government given the employment and economic significance of the company, though this is unlikely to succeed. (4) Liquidation — sell assets; not ideal given the strong competitive position, but a rational last resort.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the possible ways the company could survive the next 6–24 months?

categories.name: Wait it out / market recovery
ideas: Competitor attrition — smaller, higher-cost firms go bankrupt first, reducing supply and lifting prices
Housing tracks GDP; stimulus packages (e.g., 2009 ARRA) will eventually revive construction demand
Client is best-positioned to outlast the downturn as the lowest-cost producer

categories.name: Cash injection
ideas: Owning family injects equity capital directly to extend cash runway
Family buys out distressed competitors at steep discounts to consolidate market share
Seek bank financing or credit facility using assets as collateral
Bring in a private equity partner or strategic investor

categories.name: Government support
ideas: Appeal to Canadian federal or provincial government for a bailout or low-interest loan
Argue economic/employment significance to secure bridge financing

categories.name: Liquidation / wind-down
ideas: Sell equipment, land leases, and inventory at market value
Partial liquidation of non-core assets to generate near-term cash
Orderly wind-down if no viable path to survival is found

categories.name: Revenue stretch (likely infeasible but worth testing)
ideas: Explore new geographic markets (e.g., Mexico) — likely too slow given 6-month runway
Sell sawdust byproduct more aggressively — already a revenue stream, limited upside
Direct sales to builders bypassing Chicago warehouse — margin improvement but operationally complex

recommendation: The most viable path is a combination of injecting family capital to extend the cash runway and waiting out the downturn, relying on the company's lowest-cost position to outlast competitors
As a secondary option, the family could use available cash to acquire distressed competitors at a discount, consolidating market share ahead of the recovery
Liquidation should be a last resort, given the company's strong competitive position as the lowest-cost producer with 1/3 market share
risks: The family may refuse to inject cash given current market uncertainty
Recovery timing is unknown — prices may not rebound within a manageable timeframe even after competitors fail
A government bailout is unlikely to materialize quickly enough
Waiting out the downturn requires precise cash management; any unexpected cost spike could accelerate insolvency
next_steps: Conduct a detailed review of all revenue and cost drivers to confirm no efficiency opportunities have been missed
Begin building the financial case (NPV of waiting vs. liquidating) to present to the owning family
Commission a market analysis of competitor cash positions and failure timelines to validate the 'last firm standing' thesis
Explore government engagement channels for potential bridge financing or loan guarantees
